procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 19.04.2018 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in APP Nos. 4080 and 32494 of 2009 quashing the criminal proceedings against the respondent no. 1.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Allahabad stayed the arrest of respondent no. 1 vide order dated 23.07.2008 in Petition No. 10181 of 2008. The High Court then quashed the criminal proceedings against respondent no. 1 in APP Nos. 4080 and 32494 of 2009.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court's order quashing the criminal proceedings should be set aside because there was merit in his appeal. The Supreme Court agreed with the appellant, allowed the appeals, and set aside the High Court's order.

directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside.
Judgment and Order of the High Court quashing the criminal proceedings against the respondent no. 1 may not be interfered with.
We dispose of the present appeals in light of the aforesaid directions.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court, while deciding the issue of sanction, should confine itself only to the allegations in the complaint.

law.fact_text: The question of whether sanction is required for prosecution can be raised and considered at any stage of the proceedings.
relevant_text: Question of sanction may arise at any stage of proceedings.
Whether sanction is necessary or not may have to be determined from stage to stage.

It is well settled that question of sanction under Section 197 of the Code can be raised any time after the cognizance; maybe immediately after cognizance or framing of charge or even at the time of conclusion of trial and after conviction as well.

law.fact_text: A court is not required to limit its consideration to only the allegations made in the complaint when deciding the issue of sanction.
relevant_text: While deciding the issue of sanction, it is not necessary for the Court to confine itself to the allegations made in the complaint.
in considering the question whether or not sanction for prosecution was required, it is not necessary for the Court to confine itself to the allegations in the complaint

law.fact_text: The court can take into account all the material available on record at the time the question of sanction is being considered.
relevant_text: It can take into account all the material on record available at the time when such a question is raised and falls for the consideration of the Court.
the Court must consider not only the allegations made in the complaint but also other materials available on record.

application.fact_text: The Court reasoned that a complaint might not initially reveal that the alleged act was done in the discharge of official duty.
relevant_text: There might arise situations where the complaint or the police report may not disclose that the act constituting the offence was done or purported to be done in the discharge of official duty.

application.fact_text: Facts that establish the need for sanction can emerge later in the proceedings, through police or judicial inquiry, or during the trial itself.
relevant_text: However, the facts subsequently coming to light may establish the necessity for sanction.
The necessity may reveal itself in the course of the progress of the case.

application.fact_text: Because the need for sanction can become apparent at any time, the issue must be assessed based on the material available at that specific stage, not just the initial complaint.
relevant_text: Therefore, the question whether sanction is required or not is one that may arise at any stage of the proceeding and it may reveal itself in the course of the progress of the case.
Whether sanction is necessary or not may have to be determined from stage to stage.

application.fact_text: In some cases, the question of sanction cannot be effectively decided without allowing the defense to present evidence to show that the act was part of their official duty.
relevant_text: But there may be certain cases where it may not be possible to decide the question effectively without giving opportunity to the defence to establish that what he did was in discharge of official duty.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that a court must confine itself to the allegations in the complaint when deciding the issue of sanction. It held that the question can be considered at any stage of the proceedings, and the court can take into account all material on record at the time the issue is raised, as facts establishing the need for sanction may emerge after the complaint is filed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the question of an act being done 'purporting to be in execution of his duty' by a public servant is a question of fact to be determined based on the act and attendant circumstances, without any hard and fast rule.

application.sentence: The Supreme Court determined that the question of whether a public servant's act was done 'purporting to be in execution of his duty' is fundamentally a question of fact.
references:
that the question of whether or not the act complained of is one 
“purporting to be done in execution of his duty” as a public servant 
is substantially one of fact which is to be determined with reference 
to the act complained of along with the attendant circumstances.

In other words, the question whether a particular act is done by a 
public servant in the discharge of his official duty is substantially 
one of fact, which is to be determined in the unique circumstances 
of each case.

application.sentence: The Court explicitly stated that it would be unwise and undesirable to establish any 'hard and fast tests' or a 'universal rule' for this determination.
references:
It 
would not be wise nor desirable to lay down any hard and fast tests 
in this regard.

There cannot be any universal rule 
to determine whether there is a reasonable connection 
between the act done and the official duty, nor is it 
possible to lay down any such rule.

application.sentence: Instead of a rigid rule, the decision must be made by examining the specific act in question along with the 'attendant circumstances' unique to each case.
references:
that the question of whether or not the act complained of is one 
“purporting to be done in execution of his duty” as a public servant 
is substantially one of fact which is to be determined with reference 
to the act complained of along with the attendant circumstances.

In other words, the question whether a particular act is done by a 
public servant in the discharge of his official duty is substantially 
one of fact, which is to be determined in the unique circumstances 
of each case.

application.sentence: The focus of the inquiry is on the 'quality of the act' itself to see if it falls within the scope and range of the public servant's official duties.
references:
It is the quality of the 
act which is important and the protection of this section 
is available if the act falls within the scope and range 
of his official duty.

application.sentence: As a guideline for this factual analysis, the Court offered a test: to consider if the public servant could have been charged with dereliction of duty for failing to perform the act in question.
references:
One safe and sure 
test in this regard would be to consider if the omission 
or neglect on the part of the public servant to commit the 
act complained of could have made him answerable for 
a charge of dereliction of his official duty.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, holding that whether a public servant's act purports to be in the execution of their duty is a question of fact. This determination cannot be governed by a hard and fast rule but must be decided on a case-by-case basis, considering the specific act and its surrounding circumstances.

cases.case_name: Amrik Singh v. State of Pepsu
cases.principle: The test to determine if an act was committed in the discharge of official duty is to consider if the omission or neglect by the public servant to commit the act complained of could have made him answerable for a charge of dereliction of his official duty. If the answer is affirmative, the act is considered to be in the discharge of official duty.

cases.case_name: Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli v. State of Bombay
cases.principle: The test to determine if an act was committed in the discharge of official duty is to consider if the omission or neglect by the public servant to commit the act complained of could have made him answerable for a charge of dereliction of his official duty. If the answer is affirmative, the act is considered to be in the discharge of official duty.

cases.case_name: Raghunath Anant Govilkar v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: Explained in detail the test that an act is considered to be in the discharge of official duty if the omission or neglect by the public servant to commit that act could have made him answerable for a charge of dereliction of his official duty.

cases.case_name: Birbal Nath v. State of Rajasthan
cases.principle: Reiterated the position of law that the test to determine if an act is connected to official duty is whether the public servant's omission to perform the act would have made him answerable for dereliction of duty.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The principle of law as explained in Raghunath Anant Govilkar v. State of Maharashtra [(2008) 11 SCC 289] is the guiding legal rule.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The determination of whether a public servant's alleged criminal act was done while 'acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty,' thus requiring sanction for prosecution, is fundamentally a question of fact. This question cannot be answered by a hard and fast rule but must be decided based on the specific act and its attendant circumstances in each case. The necessity for sanction may not be apparent from the initial complaint and can emerge as the case progresses and more facts come to light. Therefore, a court should not confine its inquiry to the complaint alone and it is an error to quash proceedings at a preliminary stage without a full factual determination.
legal_tests_applied: The question of whether a particular act is done by a public servant in the discharge of his official duty is substantially one of fact, which is to be determined in the unique circumstances of each case.

The sine qua non for the applicability of this section is that the offence charged, be it one of commission or omission, must be committed by the public servant either in his official capacity or under the color of the office held by him such that there is a direct or reasonable connection between the act and the official duty.
The necessity for sanction may reveal itself in the course of the progress of the case, and is not determined solely by the allegations in the complaint at the outset.
policy_considerations: It would not be wise nor desirable to lay down any hard and fast tests in this regard [determining if an act was in execution of duty].

The expression 'any offence alleged to have been committed by him while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty' must neither be construed narrowly nor widely and the right approach would be to arrive at a balance between the two extremes.
